title: In-Memory Database with TTL Backups
prompt:
Build an in-memory database of string keys, each containing string field/value pairs.

### Basic operations

Implement `set(key, field, value)`, `get(key, field)`, `delete(key, field)`, `scan(key)`, and `scan_by_prefix(key, prefix)`. Missing reads return `None`; delete returns whether a field existed. Scans return `field(value)` strings in lexicographic field order.

### Time and expiry

Add `set_at(key, field, value, timestamp)` and `set_at_with_ttl(key, field, value, timestamp, ttl)`, plus timestamped `get_at`, `delete_at`, `scan_at`, and `scan_by_prefix_at`. Timestamps are nonnegative integers, supplied in nondecreasing order; TTLs are positive integers. A TTL value exists in `[timestamp, timestamp + ttl)`. Basic and timestamped operations are not mixed in one scenario.

### Backup and restore

`backup(timestamp)` snapshots only live values and their remaining TTLs. `restore(timestamp, timestamp_to_restore)` replaces data with the latest backup at or before `timestamp_to_restore`, restarting its remaining TTLs at `timestamp`. With no qualifying backup, leave data unchanged. Backups must remain independent of later changes.

Target average O(1) point operations and O(f log f) scans over f fields. Invalid inputs may be rejected with `assert`.

example.reasoning: The backup captures five units of TTL remaining at time 23, so restoration at time 40 expires at time 45.
